title: Symmetric Group
body:
$S_n$: **all** bijections of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ to itself, under composition. It is the largest
[[Permutation Group]] on $n$ symbols, and every other one is a [[Subgroup]] of it.

$$|S_n| = n!$$

which is the [[Permutation]] count $P(n,n)$ from [[DISCRETE MATH]] read as the size of a group.
The counting course asks how many arrangements there are; this course puts an operation on that
set and asks what structure it has. Same $n!$, and it is the whole bridge between the two senses
of the word.

## Small cases

| $n$ | $\lvert S_n\rvert$ | Notes |
|---|--:|---|
| 1 | 1 | trivial |
| 2 | 2 | $\{e, (1\,2)\}$, cyclic, abelian |
| 3 | 6 | the **smallest non-abelian group**; equals $D_3$, the symmetries of a triangle |
| 4 | 24 | the rotations of a cube, if you like the geometry |
| 5 | 120 | $A_5$ inside it is simple, which is where solvability by radicals dies |

$S_3$ is the example to keep in your head. It has three transpositions and two 3-cycles, and
$(1\,2)(1\,3) \neq (1\,3)(1\,2)$ is the shortest proof in the course that groups need not commute.

## Structure worth remembering

- **Generated by transpositions.** Any rearrangement is a sequence of swaps, which is
  bubble sort restated: see [[Sequential Sorting]]. The adjacent transpositions
  $(1\,2), (2\,3), \dots$ alone are enough.
- **Parity splits it exactly in half.** Even permutations form the [[Alternating Group]] $A_n$ of
  order $n!/2$; the odd ones are the other [[Coset]] and are not a subgroup, since odd composed
  with odd is even.
- **Cayley's theorem** says every group of order $n$ embeds in $S_n$. So $S_n$ is not one group
  among many, it is the container for all of them at that size.
- **Conjugacy classes are cycle types.** Two permutations are conjugate exactly when their cycle
  structures match, so the classes are indexed by the partitions of $n$.

## Why $n!$ is the number CS keeps hitting

$|S_n|$ growing factorially is the reason brute force over orderings is hopeless. Checking every
[[Hamiltonian Cycle]] means checking a subset of $S_n$, and $n!$ outruns $2^n$ and everything
else the [[Time Complexity]] ladder has; that is the practical face of [[NP-Complete]]. The
$\Omega(n\log n)$ lower bound for comparison sorting is the same group counted differently: a
decision tree must distinguish all $n!$ possible input orders, so it needs $\log_2(n!)$ levels.
[[Sequential Sorting]] carries that proof.
